notes.b: Rivers are useful, so people change them. Every change alters how the river's processes work: its velocity (speed of flow), erosion (wearing away of bed and banks), transport (carrying of material), deposition (dropping of material) and flooding.
points: Reasons for interfering include making electricity, supplying water, irrigation (watering crops), navigation (letting boats travel), draining farmland and protecting towns from flooding.
The three measures studied here are hydro-electric dams, canalisation and flood control, each with Irish and international examples.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to examine the impact on river processes. Explain what each measure does to velocity, erosion, transport, deposition and flooding, and do not only list costs and benefits.

notes.b: A hydro-electric dam turns the energy of falling water into electricity. It does this by holding the river back and then releasing it in a controlled way.
points: The dam stores water in a reservoir (an artificial lake behind the dam), and the water is then released so that it falls through turbines (wheels that spin and drive generators).
The drop in height of the water (the head) gives the power, so a greater drop means more energy from the same water.

notes.b: Upstream of a dam the river meets still water in the reservoir. This changes its processes completely, because a river can only carry material while it keeps moving.
points: Velocity falls to near zero in the reservoir, so the river deposits its load (the sand, silt and stones it was carrying) there.
The reservoir slowly fills with sediment, a process called sedimentation, which reduces its capacity (how much water it can hold).
A delta (a fan of deposited sediment) can build where the river enters the reservoir, because that is where the flow slows and drops its load.

notes.h: Hydro-electric dams: impacts downstream and on flow
notes.b: Below the dam the river has lost its sediment and its natural rhythm of floods and low flows. Both changes alter erosion and deposition.
points: Water released from the dam is clear of sediment, so it has spare energy and erodes the bed and banks below the dam. This is called clear-water erosion.
The floodplain (the flat land beside the river) and delta receive no new silt, so deltas and coasts erode because nothing replaces the material lost.
Discharge (the volume of water flowing past a point) is regulated, so natural floods and low flows are evened out.
Less flooding means less deposition on the floodplain, because floodwater is what normally lays down silt there.
Where water is diverted out of the old channel, the bypassed channel carries much less water.
Dams block migrating salmon and eels, which cannot pass the wall. Fish passes (routes around the dam) and trapping and transporting fish around dams are responses.
notes.tip: For impact on processes, give the sequence: velocity falls in the reservoir, so deposition happens there; the clear water below the dam then erodes the bed and banks; and the floodplain and delta get no new silt.

notes.b: The Shannon Scheme is one power station at Ardnacrusha, near Limerick, fed by a weir and a canal. It is not a series of dams.
points: It was built 1925–1929 by the German firm Siemens for the Irish Free State, and it was Ireland's first large hydro-electric station.

Parteen Weir (a low barrier across the river) diverts most of the Shannon's water into a headrace canal to Ardnacrusha. A tailrace (the channel carrying used water away) returns it to the river near Limerick.
Lough Derg's level is controlled by Parteen Weir, so the lough acts as the scheme's reservoir.
The original channel between Parteen and Limerick, the Old River Shannon, carries much less water because most of it is diverted.
Salmon and eel stocks declined. The ESB built a fish pass, and it traps silver eels (adult eels migrating downstream) upstream and transports them past the dam.
notes.tip: Describe it as one power station at Ardnacrusha fed by Parteen Weir and a canal. Do not call it a series of dams from Parteen to Limerick, and do not call Parteen Weir a dam producing power.

notes.b: Ardnacrusha is not the only Irish example. Four more dams and power stations can be named in an answer.
points: Poulaphouca dam, River Liffey: created the Blessington Lakes reservoir, Co. Wicklow. It generates electricity and supplies drinking water to Dublin.
Inniscarra and Carrigadrohid dams, River Lee, Co. Cork.
Cathaleen's Fall power station, River Erne, at Ballyshannon, Co. Donegal.

notes.h: Aswan High Dam: reservoir and benefits
notes.b: The Aswan High Dam is the main international case study. It holds back the Nile in a huge reservoir to give Egypt control over a river that once flooded and shrank unpredictably.
points: Aswan High Dam, River Nile, Egypt, was completed in 1970. Its reservoir is Lake Nasser, which extends into Sudan.
Benefits are flood control, year-round irrigation (which allows more than one crop a year), hydro-electricity, and protection from drought.

notes.h: Aswan High Dam: impacts on river processes and people
notes.b: The dam's effects follow from the same processes as any dam: trapped sediment, clear-water erosion and regulated flow. They then spread into farming, fishing, health and settlement.
points: Silt is trapped in Lake Nasser, so farmers downstream rely on artificial fertilisers instead of the natural silt that floods once left.
The river bed below the dam is scoured (worn away) by clear water, which has spare energy to erode.
The Nile delta coast is eroding, e.g. at the Rosetta promontory (a headland on the delta coast), because no new sediment arrives to replace what the sea removes.
The sardine fishery off the delta in the Mediterranean declined sharply.
Irrigated land suffers waterlogging (soil saturated with water) and salinisation (a build-up of salt in the soil).
Perennial irrigation canals (canals that hold water all year) spread the disease schistosomiasis (bilharzia).
Nubian people were displaced, and the temples of Abu Simbel were moved to higher ground.
notes.tip: A 30-mark answer needs the process changes, so link each impact to its cause: trapped silt means downstream farmers need artificial fertilisers and the delta coast erodes, and clear water scours the bed below the dam.

notes.b: The Three Gorges Dam is a second international example, built on the Yangtze to produce power and to reduce floods.
points: Three Gorges Dam, Hubei province, China, is the world's largest power station by installed capacity.
It was completed in 2006 and fully operational in 2012, and over one million people were relocated.
It aims to reduce flood peaks downstream, because the Yangtze floods of 1998 killed thousands.
It traps sediment that once reached the river's lower course and delta, so those areas receive less of the sediment they depended on.

notes.h: Canalisation: what it is and its purposes
notes.b: Canalisation modifies an existing river channel. It is not the same as building a canal.
points: Methods are straightening, deepening and widening the channel, sometimes lining it with concrete, cutting through meanders (bends in the river), dredging (scooping sediment from the bed) and building locks and weirs for navigation.
Purposes are navigation, faster drainage of land, and flood control.
notes.tip: Do not describe the Grand Canal or the Royal Canal as canalisation of a river. They are artificial canals, and canalisation means modifying an existing river channel.

notes.b: Making a river straighter and smoother makes the water move faster. Almost every other effect follows from that rise in velocity.
points: A straighter, shorter course has a steeper gradient (slope) and less friction (drag from the bed and banks), so velocity rises.
Water and floods are passed downstream faster, so flood peaks downstream are higher and arrive sooner.
Faster flow has more energy, so it erodes the bed and banks.
Where the channel widens or the flow slows again, deposition increases and dredging is needed to keep the channel clear.
Meanders, oxbow lakes (cut-off loops of old meander), pools and riffles (deeper and shallower stretches of the bed) are lost, and the river is cut off from its floodplain.
notes.tip: Explain the chain in order: a straighter course gives a steeper gradient and less friction, so velocity rises, which increases erosion, passes flood peaks downstream faster and increases deposition where the flow slows.

notes.b: Canalisation has been used for drainage and navigation in Ireland and for shortening and straightening big rivers abroad.
points: Arterial drainage (deepening and straightening main rivers to drain land) was carried out by the Office of Public Works (OPW) under the Arterial Drainage Act 1945, e.g. the Moy and Boyne schemes. Rivers were deepened and straightened mainly to drain farmland, not to protect towns.
Arterial drainage effects were changes to fish spawning beds, bank erosion and downstream flooding.
Mississippi: cut-offs (new short channels across bends) made by the US Army Corps of Engineers shortened the river.
Rhine: the Upper Rhine was straightened in the 19th century under Johann Gottfried Tulla, which sped flood waves downstream and caused the bed to erode downward.
Navigation in Ireland: locks and weirs on the Shannon Navigation control water levels and slow the flow.
notes.tip: Arterial drainage was mainly to drain farmland, not to protect towns, so say that in an Irish example.

notes.b: Flood control measures respond to the causes of river flooding, so it helps to know what those causes are.
points: Prolonged or intense rain, and saturated ground (soil that is already full of water and cannot absorb more), send water into rivers faster than they can carry it.
Urban surfaces and drains speed runoff (water flowing over land into rivers). Deforestation and drainage of bogs and farmland upstream add to it.
Building on floodplains puts homes in the path of floodwater.

notes.b: Hard engineering uses built structures to hold floodwater back or move it away. Each one changes river processes, and some pass the problem on downstream.
points: Embankments and levees (raised banks) confine flow to the channel, so deposition raises the bed and the banks must be raised again.
With embankments and levees the floodplain gets no silt, and failure gives sudden, severe floods.
Flood walls and demountable (removable) barriers protect towns.
Dams and reservoirs store floodwater.
Dredging and deepening increase channel capacity, but the flow is faster and downstream flooding can increase.
Relief (bypass) channels take floodwater around the town.
notes.tip: For each hard measure give its effect on processes as well as its purpose, for example levees confine flow so deposition raises the bed, and dredging increases capacity but speeds flow and can increase downstream flooding.

notes.b: Soft engineering works with the river instead of against it. It slows water or gives it space, so natural processes carry on.
points: Floodplain zoning uses planning controls on building, so that homes are kept off land that floods.
Afforestation (planting trees) upstream works through interception (leaves catching rain), which slows runoff.
Wetlands and bogs can be restored, and washlands (land that is allowed to flood) give the river more room.
Flood forecasting and warning give people time to prepare.
Effect on processes: natural flooding and floodplain deposition continue.

notes.b: Irish floods show hard engineering, dam management and flood-risk planning in practice.
points: Cork, November 2009: the River Lee flooded when the ESB released large volumes from Inniscarra dam during very heavy rain because the reservoir was full.
The releases were not the sole cause, because the rain was exceptional. The University College Cork and the city water treatment works were flooded, and many homes lost their water supply.
Clonmel, Co. Tipperary: an OPW flood relief scheme on the River Suir uses demountable barriers that are put in place when floods are forecast.
December 2015: Storm Desmond caused prolonged flooding on the Shannon, in towns such as Athlone.
CFRAM (Catchment Flood Risk Assessment and Management) is the OPW programme that maps flood risk.
notes.tip: Do not say the dam alone caused the Cork 2009 flood. The rain was exceptional, and the controversy was over the timing and volume of the releases.

notes.b: The Mississippi is the international case study for levees. It shows both what they protect and how they can fail.
points: The Great Mississippi Flood of 1927 led to the US federal levee and floodway system run by the US Army Corps of Engineers.
The 1993 flood breached many levees along the upper Mississippi and Missouri.
In August 2005 Hurricane Katrina caused levee and floodwall failures in New Orleans, and about 80% of the city flooded.
Levees stop flood silt reaching the delta, which contributes to the loss of Louisiana's coastal wetlands.

notes.b: The Netherlands shows a soft-engineering response to flooding: instead of building higher walls, it gives the river space.
points: Room for the River (Ruimte voor de Rivier), Netherlands, started after near-disastrous high water on the Rhine and Maas in 1993 and 1995.
Measures include moving dykes (embankments) back, lowering floodplains and digging side channels so the river can spread out safely.

notes.h: Evaluation of flood control and dams
notes.b: Exams expect a judgement, so weigh what these measures achieve against what they cost.
points: Benefits are protection of homes, electricity, navigation and water supply.
Costs are problems moved downstream, sediment starvation (rivers and deltas losing the sediment they need), habitat loss, high cost, and a false sense of security.
There is a trend towards working with natural processes.
notes.tip: Examples can be named measures (levees, dams, dredging, canalisation, soft measures), with Irish and international examples and an evaluation of each.

keyTerms.definition: The slow filling of a reservoir with sediment deposited by the river entering it.
Erosion of the bed and banks below a dam by water that is released free of sediment.
The drop in height of water through a dam, which gives hydro-electric power.
Straightening, deepening or lining an existing river channel, usually for navigation, drainage or flood control.
Deepening and straightening rivers to drain farmland, carried out by the OPW under the Arterial Drainage Act 1945.
An embankment that confines floodwater to the river channel.
A removable flood barrier put in place when a flood is forecast.
A bypass channel that takes floodwater around a town.
Planning controls that restrict building on floodplains.
Areas of land allowed to flood, giving the river more room.
The capture of rainfall by vegetation, which slows runoff.
The OPW's Catchment Flood Risk Assessment and Management programme.

questions.prompt: Examine the impact of flood control measures on river processes.
questions.model: Hard engineering measures include levees, dredging, dams and demountable barriers. Levees confine the flow to the channel, so velocity rises in the channel and deposition raises the bed, so the banks must be raised again; the floodplain receives no silt. Dredging deepens the channel and increases its capacity, but the faster flow erodes the bed and floods downstream. Dams store floodwater, so the downstream flow is reduced, but the reservoir traps sediment. Demountable barriers protect towns without changing the channel. Soft engineering measures include floodplain zoning, afforestation, restoring wetlands and washlands, and flood warning; these allow natural flooding and floodplain deposition to continue. Mississippi levees show the effects: after the 1927 and 1993 floods and the 2005 failures in New Orleans, levees stop silt reaching the delta, so the Louisiana coastal wetlands are lost. In Ireland, Cork in 2009 was flooded after releases from Inniscarra dam, and Clonmel uses demountable barriers on the River Suir. Evaluation: the measures protect homes and infrastructure, but they move problems downstream, starve the floodplain of sediment and can give a false sense of security. The trend is towards working with natural processes.

questions.prompt: Examine the impact of hydro-electric dams on river processes, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Ardnacrusha and the Aswan High Dam show the processes affected. In the reservoir, velocity falls to near zero, so the river deposits its load and the reservoir fills with sediment; at Lake Nasser, silt is trapped, so downstream farmers rely on artificial fertilisers. Downstream, the water released is clear of sediment, so it erodes the bed and banks below the dam; at Aswan the river bed is scoured. Regulated discharge evens out natural floods and low flows, so less deposition takes place on the floodplain. The lack of new silt means the Nile delta coast is eroding, for example at the Rosetta promontory. At Ardnacrusha, Parteen Weir diverts most of the Shannon's water into a canal, so the Old River Shannon carries much less water. Dams block migrating fish: at Ardnacrusha salmon and eel stocks declined, and the ESB built a fish pass and transports silver eels past the dam.

questions.prompt: Describe how canalisation affects a river.
questions.model: Canalisation straightens, deepens and widens an existing channel, cuts through meanders and dredges the channel, usually for navigation, faster drainage of land and flood control. A straighter, shorter course has a steeper gradient and less friction, so velocity increases. Water and floods pass downstream faster, so flood peaks are higher and arrive sooner. Faster flow erodes the bed and banks. Where the channel widens or the flow slows, deposition increases and dredging is needed. Meanders, oxbow lakes, pools and riffles are lost, and the river is cut off from its floodplain. The Rhine, straightened in the 19th century under Johann Gottfried Tulla, shows the downward erosion of the bed and the faster flood waves. In Ireland, arterial drainage under the Arterial Drainage Act 1945 deepened and straightened the Moy and Boyne to drain farmland, with effects on fish spawning beds, bank erosion and downstream flooding.
